# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 98 — The EMET Bible (Literal)

**Translator:** EMET | **Source:** Codex Athous, Shepherd of Hermas 98 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_098_page_001.jpg

---

## Similitude 9, Chapter 15

**1** "But the spotted stones — who are they?" **2** "These," he said, "are those who have believed and have the greater part of their faith, but they also have part of the riches of this world; **3** when affliction comes, because of their riches and the pressing of business these people deny the Lord." **4** I said to him, "When then, Lord, will they be fit for the building of the tower?" **5** "When," he said, "the wealth that leads their souls astray is cut away from them. **6** But if they repent first, they shall be fit; for just as the round stone, unless it is cut and something taken away from it, cannot become square, so also those who have wealth — unless from their riches they lose something — they cannot be suitable for the Lord." **7** "Understand this first by yourself: when you were rich you were unprofitable; now you are useful and profitable for the life of God, because you have been made needy. Be useful to God! For even you yourself are used from the same stones." **8** "But the other spotted stones — those with the white spots — who are they?" **9** "These are those who departed from God and blasphemed, and became betrayers of the servants of God. **10** For these there is no repentance, but death. Therefore they are black — for their kind is already death." **11** "But those who gave back half-withered and cracked stones — who are they?" **12** "These are those who always agreed with one another and harbored no grudges. They rejoiced greatly when they saw one another. **13** On this account their stones were pulled partly out of the tower. But because of their love for one another and their mutual harmony, they were put back again."

---

*EMET: the personal address to Hermas in v. 7 is remarkable — the Shepherd directly applies the stone-theology to Hermas himself, identifying him as one who has been impoverished for usefulness.*
